rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 <U+2013> the authors compare their own ET-based irrigation calculations (OpenET ensemble and six models, gridMET, AIM) with farmer records (239 field-years) and Kansas WIMAS flowmeter data at field, water right group and management area scales (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-8).
rows.notes: The study does not report any result of its own on water savings produced by data-supported enforcement of the 20% pumping reduction. The 26-31% withdrawal reduction in the SD-6 LEMA is cited from Deines et al. 2019, Drysdale and Hendricks 2018, Butler et al. 2020 and Whittemore et al. 2023 (Section 2.1.2), not measured here. Moreover, the LEMA was enforced through flowmeters, not remotely sensed ET; the study's own finding is that ET-based calculations can approximate reported irrigation (bias 1.6-4.9% at field scale) but that model variability exceeds the conservation signal, i.e. it only tests a precondition (ability to estimate irrigation from remote sensing) of the claimed data-driven conservation effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 <U+2013> own comparison of ET-based irrigation calculations with farmer irrigation records and statewide flowmeter database at three spatial scales (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-8).
rows.notes: The study reports no yield or crop production data of its own. The statement that the LEMA had only minor negative impacts on yield and none on profitability is cited from Golden (2018) in Section 2.1.2. The study's own results concern the accuracy of remotely sensed ET for estimating irrigation volumes, not the effect of data-driven regulation on productivity; this is at most a precondition of the claimed effect.

notes: Full text available (supplementary figures S1-S6 not included). The study is a methodological accuracy/uncertainty assessment of OpenET-based irrigation estimates in Kansas; the review's claim about water savings and yield under the SD-6 LEMA relies on background literature cited within the study rather than on the study's own findings.
